name: Celeriac “Cacio e Pepe”
why: Celeriac is peaking right now, and this is a genuinely fresh twist on a classic — silky celeriac purée replaces the usual pecorino-heavy base, giving the pasta a nutty sweetness that plays off the black pepper. Minimal faff, vegetarian, and a great technique to add to your repertoire.
author: Henry
ingredients: Approx. 200ml whole milk (just enough to cover the celeriac in the pan)
55g Pecorino Romano (30-month aged if you can find it), finely grated + extra to finish

steps: Peel and chop the celeriac into small cubes.
Bash the black pepper in a pestle and mortar — you want it rough and ready, not powdery. Texture is king.
Melt the butter in a small pan and add the celeriac cubes. Let them sizzle for a couple of minutes.
Cover the celeriac with the milk, bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat and cover with a lid left slightly ajar for 15 minutes until the celeriac is soft.
Bring a big pan of salted water to a rolling boil — sea-salty levels. Cook the pasta 1 minute short of al dente.
4 minutes before the pasta is done, warm the olive oil and crushed black pepper in a separate pan on low heat and let them infuse — don't let the pepper burn.

Once the celeriac is cool enough to handle, scoop the cubes into a blender (leave most of the excess milk behind) and blitz with the salt and a squeeze of lemon until completely smooth. If it looks split, it will come together once blended — no drama.
Drain the pasta, reserving 150ml of the cooking water first.
Tip the drained pasta into the pepper-infused oil, add 5 big spoons of the celeriac purée and turn the heat up.
Add the pecorino and a splash of the reserved pasta water. Stir vigorously until glossy, thick and saucy — adding pasta water a spoonful at a time until the sauce clings to the pasta.
Taste and season carefully — the pecorino is very salty, so hold back on extra salt.
Serve immediately with more grated pecorino on top.

pro_tips: Pecorino + pasta water = a salty situation. Don't salt the purée or pasta water aggressively until the very end, then correct to taste.
Want to really annoy tradition? Add a splash of white wine to the celeriac milk — it deepens the nuttiness and no one will be the wiser.
